reading.body:
Government AI activity is now a matter of public record: federal agencies disclose what they run, GAO audits those inventories, and 2,425 state AI bills are tracked to their source.

The pattern is layered oversight. GAO reviews federal AI inventories and management, state legislation is tracked bill by bill, and international indexes from Oxford Insights, OECD.AI, and Stanford HAI compare national readiness, strategies, and policy execution. This makes government AI adoption measurable and auditable, which shapes where and how public-sector systems can operate.

What this record does not show is the physical layer. The Oxford Insights index scores infrastructure as one dimension, but no scores or infrastructure findings appear here. The data covers governance, law, and policy, not the compute, buildings, or power behind the systems being governed.

summary: Federal AI use is publicly inventoried; GAO audits it, and the state legislatures writing AI law are tracked on this site.

analysis.body:
The clearest measured picture of AI in government comes from the Government Accountability Office, which found that 20 of 23 agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned artificial intelligence use cases, while three agencies reported not having uses for AI. Most of those use cases were in the planning phase rather than production, and in about 200 instances agencies reported they were currently using AI. Reported uses included analyzing data from cameras and radar to identify border activities, analyzing photographs from drones, and targeting scientific specimens for planetary rovers, with NASA and the Department of Commerce reporting the highest number of use cases.

The GAO also documented problems with the underlying record. Its analysis of agency inventories identified instances of incomplete and inaccurate data: five agencies provided comprehensive information for each reported use case while the other 15 had instances of incomplete and inaccurate data, some inventories omitted required data elements such as the AI life cycle stage, and two inventories included AI uses later determined by the agencies not to be AI. On compliance, ten of 23 agencies implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, 12 implemented some but not all, and one was exempt. Commerce and the General Services Administration fully implemented selected requirements, with Commerce creating a plan to develop AI technical standards and GSA establishing an AI Center of Excellence, while the Office of Management and Budget had not yet developed guidance for the acquisition and use of AI and the Office of Personnel Management had not yet established or updated an occupational category for employees performing AI work. The Office of Science and Technology Policy did not communicate its designation of which agencies were expected to fulfill specific AI requirements. The President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for nondefense research and development investment in AI.

The most visible recent deployment is America.gov, launched September 29, 2026 by the General Services Administration and the National Design Studio under an executive order, per this site's tracking. It answers questions in plain language from about 29,000 government websites, running on Google Gemini and xAI Grok. Phase 1 finds information, and Phase 2, planned for 2027 with Login.gov, is to handle applications and renewals. Covered services are public-facing federal services that serve more than 100,000 users in a 12-month period and can be accessed or applied for online, with tax filing services provided by the Internal Revenue Service and national-security-sensitive services provided by the Department of War and the Intelligence Community excluded. The site notes America.gov offers no public API and its terms bar automated agents, so it is tracked as a deployment, not a source.

The regulatory posture is being written mostly at the state level. This site's AI laws tracker counts 6,049 artificial intelligence bills across 53 jurisdictions, refreshed daily from the LegiScan legislative database, and a comparison of enrolled text covered 113 measures across 28 states, reviewed on September 18, 2026. Only two states passed a broad law reaching consequential decisions across sectors, Colorado in CO SB189 and Texas in TX HB149; every other measure names one setting, such as a companion chatbot, a political ad, an insurance prior authorization, a classroom or a state agency. Where the stakes are personal, the recurring rule is that AI may assist but may not be the only decider: insurers cannot deny care on an algorithm alone, AI cannot deliver therapy or present itself as a licensed clinician, it cannot be the sole instructor of a college course or score a teacher evaluation, and New York requires meaningful human review before agencies automate benefit decisions. No state in this set created a new agency to enforce AI law; the attorney general enforces the larger laws, often exclusively, and several states declare a violation to be an unfair or deceptive trade practice under their consumer protection act.

On the international side, the sources describe monitoring infrastructure more than measured adoption. The OECD Artificial Intelligence Policy Observatory helps countries shape trustworthy AI with the OECD AI Principles and gives access to 900+ national AI policies and initiatives, live data about AI and a blog about AI policy, and organisations developing advanced AI systems can participate by submitting a report to facilitate transparency and comparability of risk mitigation measures. Oxford Insights describes helping governments increase the impact of their public services through empowering teams and harnessing technology, and this site describes its Government AI Readiness Index as scoring nearly every country on policy capacity, governance, infrastructure, and public-sector adoption. Stanford HAI's AI Index is described here as carrying the government and policy track, including legislation counts, national strategy execution, and public-sector procurement, and Stanford HAI states that this year's Index reveals a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared we are to manage it, with the frameworks needed to govern, evaluate, and understand the technology falling behind.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material points to a few practical takeaways. The federal record shows that most planned use cases have not reached production and that inventory data is often incomplete, so internal tracking deserves attention before scaling. The state law comparison concludes that no two states wrote the same law but the same choices keep appearing, and that building to the common core covers the duties that recur most often: tell people when they are dealing with AI, keep a qualified person in any decision about health, employment, benefits or education, have a crisis protocol and know the age of your user if your product holds a conversation, and keep records of what the system does, because the attorney general is the enforcer you are most likely to meet. The sources do not report ROI figures for government AI deployments, so nothing here supports a return estimate.

https://oecd.ai/.brief: OECD.AI describes itself as a policy observatory that helps countries shape trustworthy AI in line with the OECD AI Principles, and says it offers access to more than 900 national AI policies and initiatives, live data about AI and a blog on AI policy. It invites organisations developing advanced AI systems to take part by submitting a report, saying that sharing information would help make risk mitigation measures more transparent and comparable. The observatory states that the GPAI initiative and OECD member countries' work on AI combined under the GPAI brand into one integrated partnership. Its stated purpose is to help AI actors build and use systems that respect human rights and are fair, transparent, explainable, robust, secure and safe.

https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-1059.brief: GAO reported that federal agencies have begun implementing AI, which is defined as computing systems that “learn” how to improve their performance, but many policy requirements remain unmet. Twenty of 23 agencies listed about 1,200 AI use cases, most still in planning and only roughly 200 in production, and inventories often omitted required data such as life-cycle stage or releasability. While Commerce and the GSA fully met selected requirements, agencies like OMB, OPM, and OSTP did not, and only ten agencies met all their AI requirements, twelve met some, and one was exempt. The report notes that AI can improve government operations but also poses risks, and the FY 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for non-defense AI R&D.
